faq.a: It stabilises the ankle, provides attachment for peroneal muscles, and protects the common peroneal nerve.
faq.q: Why is the fibula important if it bears little weight?

faq.a: Most isolated mid‑shaft fractures can be managed with a well‑fitted plaster or functional brace; displaced distal fractures often need fixation to restore ankle stability.
faq.q: Can a fibular fracture heal without surgery?

faq.a: It provides rapid access but can cause pain, infection, or growth‑plate injury in children; use only after peripheral attempts fail.
faq.q: What is the risk of an intra‑osseous line in the fibula?

exam: A 22‑year‑old motorcyclist presents with lateral ankle pain after a crash – what immediate bedside steps differentiate a simple sprain from a distal fibular fracture? — Look for palpable step‑off, swelling pattern, inability to bear weight, and perform a mortise X‑ray if available.

During a ward round you find a patient with foot drop after a proximal fibular fracture – what structure is likely injured and how does it affect management? — The common peroneal nerve is stretched/compressed; monitor for recovery and consider surgical decompression if no improvement in 2 weeks.

In a low‑resource clinic you cannot obtain an ankle X‑ray; how would you decide whether to immobilise the lateral malleolus? — Use clinical criteria: palpable bony step‑off, gross deformity, inability to bear weight, and neurovascular intactness; immobilise with a splint and arrange referral.

A child needs emergency vascular access and two peripheral attempts have failed – why is the proximal fibula a suitable intra‑osseous site? — The shaft is subcutaneous, easy to locate, and the peroneal artery supplies it, allowing rapid infusion.

Explain why a distal fibular fracture can lead to chronic ankle instability if not properly reduced. — The lateral malleolus contributes to the mortise; mal‑alignment permits excessive inversion, predisposing to recurrent sprains.

What are the key differences in management between an isolated fibular shaft fracture and a fibular fracture with an associated tibial fracture (floating knee)? — Isolated shaft: casting or functional brace; floating knee: urgent orthopaedic fixation of both bones to restore alignment and prevent compartment syndrome.

A patient with sickle cell disease presents with leg pain after a fall – how does sickle cell affect fracture healing of the fibula? — Sickle cell can cause delayed union and higher infection risk; ensure adequate hydration, pain control, and monitor for osteomyelitis.

Why should a distal fibular fracture be examined for lateral ankle ligament injury? — The lateral malleolus anchors the anterior talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments; fracture may disrupt them, requiring combined fixation or ligament repair.
ai.title: Fibula Anatomy and Clinical Relevance
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The fibula is the slender lateral bone of the lower leg, providing attachment for muscles and forming the lateral malleolus. Understanding its relationships, blood supply, and common injuries is essential for bedside assessment and management in low‑resource settings.

b: Length ≈ 35 cm in adults
Forms lateral malleolus at distal end
Acts as a lever for peroneal muscles
sections.p: The fibula runs parallel to the tibia from the knee to the ankle, contributing little to weight‑bearing but crucial for ankle stability and muscle attachment.

b: Head articulates with tibia at proximal tibio‑fibular joint
Shaft is subcutaneous anteromedially for 1 cm below the tuberosity
Distal end forms the lateral malleolus, part of the ankle mortise
sections.p: It has a head, shaft, and distal end; three ossification centres (proximal, shaft, distal) fuse by age 20.

b: Deep peroneal nerve runs on anteromedial shaft
Peroneal (fibular) artery accompanies the nerve
Extensor retinaculum overlies the distal shaft
sections.p: The fibula lies lateral to the tibia and is closely related to neurovascular structures that must be protected during procedures.

b: Mid‑shaft: peroneal artery perforators
Proximal: anterior tibial artery branches
sections.p: Supplied by branches of the peroneal artery (mid‑shaft) and anterior tibial artery (proximal).

b: Superficial peroneal nerve: skin over lateral leg
Deep peroneal nerve: muscles crossing the ankle
sections.p: Sensory innervation of the subcutaneous surface is via the superficial peroneal nerve; motor innervation to attached muscles comes from the deep peroneal nerve.

b: Lateral malleolus prevents excessive inversion
Peroneus longus supports transverse arch of foot
sections.p: Provides lateral stability to the ankle, serves as a lever for eversion (peroneus longus/brevis) and assists dorsiflexion via tibialis anterior attachment.

b: Proximal fibular fracture → possible common peroneal nerve palsy
Distal fibular fracture → lateral malleolus involvement, ankle instability
Mid‑shaft fracture → easy to palpate, risk of compartment syndrome if swelling
sections.p: Fibular fractures are common in road‑traffic accidents and falls; they may indicate associated ankle ligament injury or tibial fracture. In low‑resource settings, missed distal fibular fractures can lead to ankle instability and chronic pain.

t.b: Confirms fracture location and displacement; if unavailable, clinical assessment of swelling, deformity, and neurovascular status guides management

t.a: Intra‑osseous line placement at proximal fibula
t.b: Provides rapid vascular access after two failed peripheral attempts; essential when IV access is impossible

b: Palpate head, shaft, and lateral malleolus for tenderness or step‑off
Assess dorsiflexion and eversion strength (peroneal muscles)
Test sensation over dorsum of foot (deep peroneal) and lateral leg (superficial peroneal)
Check for foot drop → suggests common peroneal nerve injury
sections.p: A focused lower‑leg exam can detect fibular injury and related neurovascular compromise.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe ankle deformity with loss of pulse
Progressive swelling with pain out of proportion (suspect compartment syndrome)
Foot drop or loss of sensation indicating nerve injury
